about: Functional Architecture of the Body (FAB) is the core first-year anatomy course in Part IA of the Cambridge Medical Sciences Tripos. It covers the topographical anatomy of the trunk (thorax, abdomen and pelvis) and the upper and lower limbs, taught mainly through cadaveric dissection and prosected specimens, with lectures (including embryology), applied anatomy sessions, digital dissection software and ultrasound scanning; head and neck anatomy is taught in the second-year Head and Neck Anatomy course. The official course pages give no exam details. The latest format document found (2023–24) set a 90-minute online paper of 80 single-best-answer questions in five sections (upper limb; neck and thorax; abdomen and pelvis; lower limb; lecture material), which is the whole 2nd MB mark, plus a Tripos-only 2-hour paper of two essays (one functional, one clinically applied), each paper being half the Tripos mark. The faculty's undated overview page still calls the first paper short-answer, which looks out of date (single-best-answer questions were introduced in 2018), so check the current form and conduct notice before your exams.
topics: Upper limb: shoulder region, axilla and brachial plexus
Upper limb: elbow, forearm, wrist and hand
Peripheral nerves: structure, injury, degeneration and repair
Body plan, embryonic folding and segmentation
Bone, joints, the vertebral column and posture
Thorax, and development of the heart, lungs and diaphragm
Abdominal wall, peritoneal cavity and gut development
Autonomic nervous system; vascular and lymphatic systems
Pelvis, perineum, continence and urogenital development
Lower limb: hip, gluteal region, knee, leg, foot and locomotion

notes.h: The shoulder region, axilla and brachial plexus
notes.body:
FAB starts with the limbs because they show the core principles of the course in an accessible form: muscles are grouped into compartments, each compartment tends to share a nerve and a blood supply, and injuries to a nerve produce a predictable pattern of weakness and sensory loss. In the dissecting room, always ask "what does this structure do, what supplies it, and what happens if it is damaged?"

The pectoral girdle
- The upper limb attaches to the axial skeleton only at the sternoclavicular joint; everything else is muscular. This gives the shoulder a huge range of movement at the cost of stability.
- The glenohumeral joint is a shallow ball-and-socket joint. The glenoid labrum deepens the socket slightly, but stability depends mainly on the rotator cuff.
- Rotator cuff: supraspinatus (abduction, especially early abduction), infraspinatus and teres minor (lateral rotation) and subscapularis (medial rotation). Their tendons blend with the joint capsule. The precise share of early abduction contributed by supraspinatus versus deltoid is still argued about; learn the classic teaching but know it is a simplification.
- Scapulothoracic movement: about a third of overall arm elevation comes from rotation of the scapula (trapezius and serratus anterior), so full elevation above the head needs both joints working together.
- Anterior dislocation is by far the most common type and can stretch the axillary nerve, which wraps round the surgical neck of the humerus.

The axilla
- A pyramidal space between the arm and chest wall, carrying the axillary artery and vein, the cords and branches of the brachial plexus and the axillary lymph nodes.
- Pectoralis minor divides the axillary artery into three parts (proximal to, behind and distal to the muscle).
- Axillary lymph nodes drain most of the breast and upper limb, which is why they are examined in breast cancer.

The brachial plexus (C5 to T1)
- Roots (ventral rami C5–T1) form three trunks: upper (C5–C6), middle (C7) and lower (C8–T1).
- Each trunk splits into anterior and posterior divisions. Anterior divisions supply flexor compartments; posterior divisions supply extensor compartments.
- Divisions form three cords named by their relation to the axillary artery: lateral, posterior and medial.
- Five main terminal branches: musculocutaneous (lateral cord), axillary and radial (posterior cord), ulnar (medial cord) and median (lateral and medial cords).
- Other key branches: long thoracic nerve (from roots C5–C7) to serratus anterior; damage gives a "winged" scapula.

Clinical patterns
- Upper trunk injury (Erb's palsy), from forcible widening of the neck–shoulder angle: the arm hangs medially rotated and adducted with the forearm pronated ("waiter's tip").
- Lower trunk injury (Klumpke's palsy), from forcible abduction of the arm: weakness of the small hand muscles and clawing; Horner's syndrome may occur if the T1 sympathetic outflow is damaged.
- Axillary nerve injury: weak abduction beyond the first few degrees and loss of sensation over the lower deltoid ("regimental badge" area).

Exam tips: draw the plexus quickly and label the cords relative to the axillary artery; link each injury to its mechanism, posture and sensory loss.

The distal upper limb is where nerve-injury questions are most common, so learn which nerve supplies each compartment and what the hand looks like when each nerve fails.

Arm and elbow
- Anterior compartment of the arm (biceps, brachialis, coracobrachialis): musculocutaneous nerve. Posterior compartment (triceps): radial nerve.
- The radial nerve winds round the back of the humerus in the radial (spiral) groove, so a mid-shaft fracture can damage it, producing wrist drop with sparing of triceps if the injury is below the branches to triceps.
- The cubital fossa contains, from lateral to medial, the biceps tendon, the brachial artery and the median nerve, with the radial nerve lying under the lateral edge of the fossa. Supracondylar fractures in children can injure the brachial artery and median nerve.
- The ulnar nerve passes behind the medial epicondyle, where it is easily knocked ("funny bone").

Forearm
- Anterior (flexor) compartment: mainly median nerve; flexor carpi ulnaris and the medial half of flexor digitorum profundus are supplied by the ulnar nerve.
- Posterior (extensor) compartment: radial nerve. Brachioradialis and extensor carpi radialis longus are supplied by the radial nerve itself above the elbow; most of the rest by its deep branch (posterior interosseous nerve).
- Pronation and supination occur at the proximal and distal radio-ulnar joints; biceps is a powerful supinator of the flexed forearm.

Wrist and carpal tunnel
- The carpal tunnel is bounded by the carpal bones and the flexor retinaculum. It contains the median nerve and nine tendons: four of flexor digitorum superficialis, four of flexor digitorum profundus and flexor pollicis longus.
- Carpal tunnel syndrome compresses the median nerve: numbness of the lateral three and a half digits on the palmar side and weakness/wasting of the thenar muscles. Sensation over the thenar eminence is usually spared because the palmar cutaneous branch passes superficial to the retinaculum.
- The scaphoid is the most commonly fractured carpal bone. Its blood supply enters distally, so the proximal pole can undergo avascular necrosis. Tenderness in the anatomical snuffbox is the classic sign.

Hand
- Median nerve: its recurrent branch supplies the thenar muscles (abductor pollicis brevis, flexor pollicis brevis, opponens pollicis), and its digital branches supply the lateral two lumbricals. The deep head of flexor pollicis brevis often receives ulnar supply.
- Ulnar nerve supplies most other intrinsic muscles: hypothenar muscles, interossei, medial two lumbricals and adductor pollicis.
- Interossei: palmar adduct (PAD) and dorsal abduct (DAB) the fingers relative to the middle finger.
- Lumbricals flex the metacarpophalangeal joints and extend the interphalangeal joints.

Classic deformities
- Ulnar nerve lesion at the wrist: "claw hand", most marked in the ring and little fingers (loss of medial lumbricals). A lesion at the elbow paradoxically gives less clawing because the medial half of flexor digitorum profundus is also paralysed (the "ulnar paradox").
- Radial nerve lesion in the arm: wrist drop.
- Median nerve lesion at the elbow: inability to flex the index (and partly the middle) finger when trying to make a fist, often called the "hand of benediction". Some sources use this eponym for the ulnar claw instead, so describe the posture rather than relying on the name.

Exam tips: for each nerve, learn origin, course, motor supply, sensory supply and the commonest site of injury; questions often give a fracture and ask for the deficit.

notes.h: Peripheral nerves: structure, injury, degeneration and repair
notes.body:
Every limb lecture depends on understanding what a peripheral nerve is made of and how it responds to injury. This topic links the dissecting room to histology and to clinical neurology.

Structure of a peripheral nerve
- A nerve is a bundle of axons, both myelinated and unmyelinated, carrying motor, sensory and autonomic fibres.
- Connective tissue sheaths: endoneurium around individual axons, perineurium around fascicles (together with endoneurial capillaries it forms the blood–nerve barrier), and epineurium around the whole nerve.
- In the peripheral nervous system, Schwann cells make myelin; each Schwann cell myelinates one internode of one axon. In the CNS, oligodendrocytes do the job and one cell myelinates many axons.
- A typical spinal nerve forms from dorsal (sensory) and ventral (motor) roots and splits into a dorsal ramus (back muscles and skin) and a ventral ramus (limbs and the front and sides of the trunk).

Dermatomes and myotomes
- A dermatome is the area of skin supplied by one spinal nerve; a myotome is the group of muscles supplied by one spinal segment.
- Useful landmarks: C6 thumb, C7 middle finger, C8 little finger, T4 nipple, T10 umbilicus, L1 groin, L4 medial leg, L5 dorsum of foot, S1 lateral foot and sole.
- Dermatome maps vary between sources because adjacent dermatomes overlap, so loss of one root rarely produces a sharp-edged area of numbness.

Classification of nerve injury (Seddon)
- Neurapraxia: conduction block with the axon intact, often due to compression or ischaemia; recovery within days to weeks.
- Axonotmesis: axons are cut but the connective tissue sheaths remain intact, so regenerating axons are guided back to their targets; recovery is usually good but slow.
- Neurotmesis: the whole nerve is divided; recovery needs surgical repair and is often incomplete.
- Sunderland later subdivided these into five grades according to which sheath is disrupted.

Wallerian degeneration
- After an axon is cut, the distal segment, cut off from the cell body, breaks down over the following days. Myelin fragments and debris are cleared by Schwann cells and recruited macrophages.
- The cell body shows chromatolysis: it swells, the nucleus moves to the periphery and Nissl substance (rough ER) disperses as the neuron switches to producing proteins for regrowth.

Regeneration
- Schwann cells in the distal stump proliferate and line up in tubes (bands of Büngner), secreting growth factors and guiding sprouts from the proximal stump.
- Regrowth is slow, commonly quoted as roughly 1 mm per day, although the rate varies with age, site and type of injury. Recovery is tested by the advancing Tinel's sign (tingling when tapping over the regenerating tip).
- Muscles denervated for too long atrophy and their motor end plates degenerate, so very proximal injuries often recover poorly.
- Misdirected regrowth can cause synkinesis or poor localisation.
- In the CNS, regeneration is much poorer, partly because of inhibitory myelin proteins and glial scarring.

Exam tips: distinguish neurapraxia, axonotmesis and neurotmesis by what is preserved; be able to explain why recovery after a proximal lesion is slower and less complete.

notes.h: Body plan, embryonic folding and segmentation
notes.body:
Embryology in FAB is there to explain adult anatomy: why nerves and vessels run where they do, why the gut hangs in a mesentery and why some congenital defects happen.

Gastrulation and the three germ layers (week 3)
- Cells of the epiblast migrate through the primitive streak to form endoderm and mesoderm; the remaining epiblast becomes ectoderm.
- Ectoderm: epidermis and the nervous system (via the neural plate and neural crest).
- Mesoderm: muscle, bone, connective tissue, the heart and blood vessels, kidneys and gonads.
- Endoderm: the lining of the gut and its glands (liver, pancreas) and of the respiratory tract.
- The notochord forms in the midline and induces the overlying ectoderm to form the neural plate (neurulation). It persists in the adult only as part of the nucleus pulposus of the intervertebral discs.

Subdivisions of the mesoderm
- Paraxial mesoderm, beside the notochord, forms somites.
- Intermediate mesoderm forms the urogenital system.
- Lateral plate mesoderm splits into a somatic (parietal) layer, which joins the ectoderm as the body wall (somatopleure), and a splanchnic (visceral) layer, which joins the endoderm as the gut wall (splanchnopleure). The space between them is the intraembryonic coelom, which becomes the pericardial, pleural and peritoneal cavities.

Folding (week 4)
- The flat disc folds in two directions. Head-to-tail folding brings the heart and septum transversum to the front of the chest region. Lateral folding brings the two sides of the body wall together in the midline.
- Folding incorporates part of the yolk sac as the gut tube: foregut, midgut and hindgut. The midgut stays connected to the yolk sac by the vitelline duct, whose persistence gives a Meckel's diverticulum.
- Defective closure of the body wall is associated with gastroschisis (gut protrudes through a defect beside the umbilicus, with no covering sac). Exomphalos (omphalocele) is different: the normally herniated midgut fails to return, leaving bowel in a membrane-covered sac at the umbilicus.

Segmentation
- Paraxial mesoderm buds off somites in pairs from head to tail. Each somite gives a sclerotome (vertebrae and ribs), a myotome (skeletal muscle) and a dermatome (dermis of the back).
- Each vertebra forms from the caudal half of one sclerotome and the cranial half of the next ("resegmentation"). That is why spinal nerves, which grow out to the middle of each segment, exit between adjacent vertebrae and why segmental muscles span two vertebrae.
- Myotomes divide into epaxial muscle (the deep back muscles, supplied by dorsal rami) and hypaxial muscle (body wall and limb muscle, supplied by ventral rami).
- Segmental identity along the axis is controlled by Hox genes, expressed in nested domains; altering their expression can change one vertebral type into another.

Limbs
- Limb buds appear in week 4–5 (upper slightly before lower) and are colonised by migrating hypaxial muscle precursors from somites, which explains why limb muscles are supplied by ventral rami through plexuses.
- The lower limb rotates medially during development, so its extensor compartment ends up facing anteriorly and its dermatomes spiral round the limb.

Exam tips: link each adult feature to its embryological origin (for example, dorsal versus ventral rami, Meckel's diverticulum, the pattern of dermatomes).

notes.h: Bone, joints, the vertebral column and posture
notes.body:
This topic covers the general principles of the skeleton and then the vertebral column, which holds the body upright, protects the spinal cord and allows movement.

Bone
- Compact (cortical) bone forms the outer shell; spongy (trabecular) bone fills the ends of long bones, with trabeculae aligned along lines of stress.
- Intramembranous ossification (bone forms directly in mesenchyme): flat bones of the skull vault and much of the clavicle. Endochondral ossification (bone replaces a cartilage model): most of the skeleton, including long bones and vertebrae.
- Long bones grow in length at the epiphyseal growth plates until these fuse after puberty.
- Bone remodels in response to load (often called Wolff's law): disuse leads to bone loss, while loading maintains or increases bone mass.
- Fractures heal through haematoma, soft (cartilaginous) callus, hard callus and remodelling.

Joints
- Fibrous (sutures, syndesmoses), cartilaginous (primary, hyaline, as in growth plates; secondary, fibrocartilaginous, as in the pubic symphysis and intervertebral discs) and synovial joints.
- Synovial joints have articular hyaline cartilage, a capsule lined by synovial membrane and synovial fluid. Stability depends on bony shape, ligaments and muscles, and there is a trade-off between stability and mobility (compare hip and shoulder).

The vertebral column
- Usually 7 cervical, 12 thoracic, 5 lumbar, 5 fused sacral and a variable small number (often 4) of coccygeal vertebrae.
- Curvatures: the primary curvatures (thoracic and sacral kyphoses) are present before birth; the secondary curvatures (cervical and lumbar lordoses) develop as the infant holds up its head and starts to stand and walk.
- A typical vertebra has a body, a vertebral arch (pedicles and laminae), spinous and transverse processes and superior and inferior articular processes forming facet joints.
- Regional features: cervical vertebrae have foramina in the transverse processes for the vertebral arteries; thoracic vertebrae have costal facets for the ribs; lumbar vertebrae have large bodies.
- Ligaments: anterior longitudinal (resists extension), posterior longitudinal, ligamentum flavum (elastic, between laminae), interspinous and supraspinous.

Intervertebral discs
- An outer annulus fibrosus of concentric fibrocartilage lamellae surrounds a gelatinous nucleus pulposus.
- Discs usually herniate posterolaterally, where the posterior longitudinal ligament is thinnest. In the lumbar spine, a posterolateral L4/L5 herniation typically compresses the L5 root (the root descending to exit below), because the L4 root has already exited above the disc.
- Spinal nerves exit through intervertebral foramina; C1–C7 exit above their vertebra, C8 below C7, and all others below the vertebra of the same number.

Posture and locomotion
- In upright standing, the line of gravity passes close to the joints, so relatively little muscle activity is needed; small postural muscles (such as soleus and the deep back muscles) make continuous corrections.
- The gait cycle has a stance phase (heel strike to toe off, roughly 60% of the cycle at normal walking speed) and a swing phase (about 40%).

Exam tips: be able to explain the root affected by a given disc herniation and to relate curvatures to development.

notes.h: Thorax, and development of the heart, lungs and diaphragm
notes.body:
The thorax is examined both from dissection (heart, lungs, mediastinum) and from the embryology lectures that explain common congenital defects.

Thoracic wall and pleura
- Twelve pairs of ribs; ribs 1–7 join the sternum directly by their costal cartilages, ribs 8–10 join the cartilage above, and ribs 11–12 are floating.
- The intercostal neurovascular bundle (vein, artery, nerve, from above down) runs in the costal groove under the lower border of each rib. Needles and chest drains are therefore placed just above the upper border of a rib.
- The parietal pleura lines the chest wall, diaphragm and mediastinum; the visceral pleura covers the lung. The costodiaphragmatic recess is the lowest part of the pleural cavity, where fluid collects.
- Breathing: the diaphragm is the main muscle of quiet inspiration. Rib elevation increases thoracic diameters ("pump handle" for the anteroposterior diameter of upper ribs, "bucket handle" for the transverse diameter of lower ribs).

Lungs and airways
- Right lung: three lobes (upper, middle, lower) separated by oblique and horizontal fissures. Left lung: two lobes, with the lingula and cardiac notch.
- The right main bronchus is wider, shorter and more vertical than the left, so inhaled foreign bodies more often enter the right side.
- Each lung is divided into bronchopulmonary segments, each with its own segmental bronchus and artery, which can be removed surgically.

Mediastinum and heart
- The mediastinum is divided into superior and inferior parts at the plane of the sternal angle (around T4/T5), where the second costal cartilage meets the sternum. The inferior mediastinum has anterior, middle (heart and pericardium) and posterior divisions.
- Fibrous pericardium encloses the heart; the serous pericardium has parietal and visceral layers with a potential space between them (cardiac tamponade if fluid accumulates).
- Coronary arteries arise from the aortic sinuses. The left coronary artery divides into the anterior interventricular (left anterior descending) and circumflex arteries; the right coronary artery usually supplies the sinoatrial and atrioventricular nodes. Coronary "dominance" is defined by which artery gives the posterior interventricular artery, and this varies between people.

Development of the heart
- The heart begins as a tube derived from splanchnic mesoderm; it starts beating around the fourth week and loops to the right.
- Septation divides the atria (septum primum and septum secundum, leaving the foramen ovale for right-to-left shunting before birth), the ventricles (muscular and membranous septum) and the outflow tract (spiral aorticopulmonary septum, partly from neural crest).
- At birth the foramen ovale closes functionally as left atrial pressure rises, and the ductus arteriosus constricts. Defects include atrial and ventricular septal defects, patent ductus arteriosus and tetralogy of Fallot.

Development of the lungs and diaphragm
- The lung bud grows from the ventral wall of the foregut; the tracheo-oesophageal septum separates trachea from oesophagus (failure gives tracheo-oesophageal fistula).
- Lung development passes through embryonic, pseudoglandular, canalicular, saccular and alveolar stages; alveoli continue to form after birth. Surfactant from type II cells is often insufficient in babies born very early, causing respiratory distress.
- The diaphragm develops from the septum transversum, the pleuroperitoneal membranes, the dorsal mesentery of the oesophagus and body-wall muscle. It is supplied by the phrenic nerve (C3–C5) because the septum transversum formed in the neck region. Failure of the pleuroperitoneal membrane to close, usually on the left, causes congenital diaphragmatic hernia.

Exam tips: learn the level of the sternal angle and what happens there; link each congenital defect to the developmental step that failed.

notes.h: Abdominal wall, peritoneal cavity and gut development
notes.body:
The abdomen is dissected layer by layer, and its arrangement only makes sense once you know how the gut developed and rotated.

The anterior abdominal wall
- Layers: skin, superficial fascia (fatty and membranous layers), external oblique, internal oblique, transversus abdominis, transversalis fascia, extraperitoneal fat and parietal peritoneum. Rectus abdominis lies in the rectus sheath formed by the aponeuroses of the three flat muscles.
- Nerve supply is segmental from the ventral rami of T7–T12 and L1 (T10 at the umbilicus).

The inguinal canal
- An oblique passage, about 4 cm long, above the medial half of the inguinal ligament, running from the deep inguinal ring (in transversalis fascia, just above the midpoint of the inguinal ligament) to the superficial ring (in the external oblique aponeurosis, above the pubic tubercle).
- It carries the spermatic cord in males and the round ligament of the uterus in females, plus the ilio-inguinal nerve.
- Indirect inguinal hernias enter the deep ring lateral to the inferior epigastric vessels, often along a patent processus vaginalis, and can descend into the scrotum. Direct hernias push through the posterior wall medial to the inferior epigastric vessels (Hesselbach's triangle) and are more common in older men.

Peritoneum
- The parietal peritoneum lines the walls; the visceral peritoneum covers organs. Intraperitoneal organs hang on mesenteries; retroperitoneal organs lie behind the peritoneum (primarily, like the kidneys, or secondarily, like most of the duodenum and the ascending and descending colon, which lost their mesentery during development).
- The greater sac and the lesser sac (omental bursa) communicate through the epiploic (omental) foramen.
- Parietal peritoneum is supplied by somatic nerves and its pain is sharp and well localised; visceral peritoneum has autonomic afferents and its pain is poorly localised.

Development of the gut
- The gut tube is divided by its blood supply: foregut (coeliac trunk) to the second part of the duodenum, including the liver, gallbladder and pancreas (the spleen is mesodermal, not foregut, but is also supplied by the coeliac trunk); midgut (superior mesenteric artery) to about two-thirds of the way along the transverse colon; hindgut (inferior mesenteric artery) to the upper anal canal.
- Visceral pain is referred by origin: foregut to the epigastrium, midgut to the periumbilical region, hindgut to the suprapubic region. This explains why early appendicitis pain is periumbilical before it moves to the right iliac fossa when the parietal peritoneum becomes inflamed.
- The stomach rotates 90° clockwise about its longitudinal axis (viewed from above), which places the left vagus anteriorly and creates the lesser sac.
- The midgut loop herniates into the umbilical cord in about week 6, rotates a total of 270° anticlockwise (viewed from the front) around the axis of the superior mesenteric artery and returns to the abdomen by about week 10–12.
- Malrotation can leave the bowel on a narrow mesentery that may twist (volvulus), a surgical emergency in infants. Failure of return gives exomphalos.

Exam tips: be able to explain the course of an indirect versus a direct inguinal hernia relative to the inferior epigastric vessels, and to use the foregut/midgut/hindgut scheme to predict blood supply and referred pain.

notes.h: Autonomic nervous system; vascular and lymphatic systems
notes.body:
These lectures cover the "plumbing and wiring" that runs through every region you dissect.

Organisation of the autonomic nervous system
- Two-neuron pathway: a preganglionic neuron in the CNS synapses with a postganglionic neuron in a ganglion, which supplies smooth muscle, cardiac muscle or glands.
- Sympathetic outflow is thoracolumbar (lateral horn of T1–L2). Parasympathetic outflow is craniosacral (cranial nerves III, VII, IX and X, and S2–S4).
- Sympathetic preganglionic fibres leave in ventral roots, pass through white rami communicantes (only T1–L2) to the sympathetic chain, and then synapse at the same level, travel up or down the chain, or pass through without synapsing as splanchnic nerves to prevertebral ganglia (coeliac, superior and inferior mesenteric).
- Postganglionic sympathetic fibres return to every spinal nerve via grey rami communicantes, so the sympathetic system reaches sweat glands, blood vessels and arrector pili throughout the body.
- The adrenal medulla is supplied directly by preganglionic sympathetic fibres; its chromaffin cells act like postganglionic neurons, releasing adrenaline (and some noradrenaline) into the blood.
- Parasympathetic ganglia lie close to or in the wall of the target organ, so preganglionic fibres are long and postganglionic fibres short.
- Transmitters: acetylcholine at all autonomic ganglia (nicotinic receptors) and at parasympathetic targets (muscarinic receptors); noradrenaline at most sympathetic targets. Sympathetic fibres to sweat glands are a notable exception and use acetylcholine.

Visceral afferents and referred pain
- Visceral pain afferents largely travel back with sympathetic fibres and enter the cord at the segments that gave the sympathetic supply, so pain is felt in the matching dermatomes (for example, cardiac pain in the T1–T4 region and down the inner arm).
- Horner's syndrome, from interruption of the sympathetic supply to the head, gives ptosis, miosis and loss of facial sweating on that side.

The vascular system
- Arteries branch to supply regions; where anastomoses exist, collateral flow can bypass a blockage (for example round the scapula or the elbow). End arteries without effective anastomoses (for example, the central artery of the retina) leave tissue vulnerable to infarction.
- Veins have valves in the limbs; contraction of surrounding muscles (the "muscle pump") drives blood towards the heart. Valve failure in superficial veins leads to varicose veins.
- Portal systems connect two capillary beds: the hepatic portal vein carries blood from the gut to the liver. Portosystemic anastomoses (lower oesophagus, rectum, umbilicus) enlarge in portal hypertension.

The lymphatic system
- Lymphatic capillaries collect excess interstitial fluid and protein, which pass through lymph nodes before returning to the venous system.
- The thoracic duct begins at the cisterna chyli in the abdomen and drains lymph from the lower body and the left upper body into the junction of the left internal jugular and subclavian veins. The right lymphatic duct drains the right side of the head, neck, thorax and right upper limb.
- Lymph nodes are relevant clinically because cancers spread along lymphatic routes and infection causes tender lymphadenopathy. Impaired drainage causes lymphoedema.

Exam tips: be able to draw a sympathetic pathway from the lateral horn to an effector in the limb and explain why visceral pain is referred.

FAB uses imaging and ultrasound scanning to connect dissected anatomy with how doctors see the living body. You should be able to recognise major structures on plain films, CT, MRI and ultrasound, and know the basic physics and limitations of each.

Plain radiography (X-ray)
- X-ray absorption increases with tissue density and, steeply, with atomic number (which is why calcium in bone and iodine or barium contrast absorb so strongly). On a radiograph, structures that absorb more appear whiter.
- Five basic densities, from dark to light: air, fat, soft tissue/fluid, bone (calcium) and metal.
- A border is seen only where two different densities meet. Loss of a normal outline (the "silhouette sign") suggests that something of soft-tissue density, such as consolidation, lies next to it, for example loss of the right heart border with right middle lobe disease.
- A standard chest film is taken posteroanterior (PA) with the patient standing; an anteroposterior (AP) film magnifies the heart, so heart size should not be judged on an AP film.
- On a chest radiograph you should identify the trachea, carina, aortic knuckle, pulmonary hila, heart borders, diaphragm domes (the right is usually higher) and costophrenic angles.

Computed tomography (CT)
- CT uses X-rays from many angles to reconstruct cross-sectional images. Densities are expressed in Hounsfield units: water 0, air about −1000, fat negative, bone high positive.
- By convention, axial images are viewed from the feet, so the patient's right is on the viewer's left.
- Intravenous contrast highlights vessels and vascular organs. CT is fast and widely used in trauma and for detecting haemorrhage, but involves a considerably higher radiation dose than a plain film.

Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI)
- MRI uses a strong magnetic field and radiofrequency pulses acting on hydrogen nuclei; there is no ionising radiation.
- On T1-weighted images fat is bright and fluid dark; on T2-weighted images fluid is bright. (Fat can also appear bright on some T2 sequences, so use fluid to tell them apart.)
- MRI gives excellent soft-tissue contrast, so it is preferred for the brain, spinal cord, discs, joints (ligaments and menisci) and pelvic organs. It is slower and contraindicated with some metallic implants.

Ultrasound
- High-frequency sound pulses are reflected at boundaries between tissues of different acoustic impedance. Fluid is anechoic (black), and bone and gas reflect almost all sound, casting acoustic shadows.
- It is cheap, portable, real-time and free of ionising radiation, so it is used in pregnancy, for the gallbladder, kidneys and vessels, and to guide needles. It is operator-dependent and limited by gas and bone.
- Doppler ultrasound measures blood flow direction and velocity.

Radiation protection and choice of test
- Ionising radiation carries a small, dose-related risk of causing cancer, so in the UK exposures must be justified and kept as low as reasonably practicable (IR(ME)R regulations). Children and pregnant women need particular care.
- Choosing a test balances the clinical question, availability, speed, radiation dose and the patient's condition.

Exam tips: practise naming structures on labelled CT and MRI slices at standard levels (for example T4, L1) and be ready to justify which modality suits a clinical question.

notes.h: Pelvis, perineum, continence and urogenital development
notes.body:
The pelvis must support the abdominal contents, allow passage of urine, faeces and (in females) a baby, and keep these exits closed until the right moment. Its development explains its arrangement and several common congenital conditions.

The bony pelvis and pelvic floor
- The pelvic girdle is formed by the two hip bones (ilium, ischium and pubis fused at the acetabulum) and the sacrum. The pelvic inlet (brim) is bounded by the sacral promontory and alae, the arcuate and pectineal lines and the pubic crests.
- Typical sex differences: the female pelvis has a wider, more oval inlet, a wider subpubic angle, ischial spines that project less into the cavity and more everted ischial tuberosities, adaptations for childbirth.
- The pelvic floor (pelvic diaphragm) is made of levator ani (puborectalis, pubococcygeus and iliococcygeus) and coccygeus. It supports the pelvic organs and contributes to continence.
- The pudendal nerve (S2–S4) supplies the external sphincters and perineal skin; it passes round the ischial spine, which is used as a landmark for pudendal nerve block in obstetrics.

Urinary continence and micturition
- The detrusor muscle of the bladder contracts under parasympathetic control (pelvic splanchnic nerves, S2–S4).
- The internal urethral sphincter at the bladder neck is smooth muscle; it is well developed in males and under sympathetic control, preventing retrograde ejaculation. The external urethral sphincter is striated muscle, supplied by the pudendal nerve and under voluntary control.
- Bladder filling is sensed by stretch receptors; voiding is coordinated by the pontine micturition centre, which relaxes the sphincters and activates the detrusor. Cortical control allows voluntary timing.
- Stress incontinence (leakage with coughing) often follows weakened pelvic floor support, for example after childbirth.

Faecal continence
- Internal anal sphincter: smooth muscle, involuntary, responsible for most of the resting tone.
- External anal sphincter: striated muscle supplied by the pudendal nerve (inferior rectal branches), under voluntary control.
- Puborectalis forms a sling round the anorectal junction, creating the anorectal angle; relaxation straightens the angle for defecation.

Development of the urinary system
- Intermediate mesoderm forms three successive kidneys: the pronephros (non-functional in humans), the mesonephros (temporarily functional) and the metanephros, the permanent kidney.
- The ureteric bud grows from the mesonephric duct into the metanephric mesenchyme (blastema). The bud forms the ureter, pelvis, calyces and collecting ducts; the mesenchyme forms the nephrons. Each induces the other.
- The kidneys "ascend" from the pelvis to the lumbar region; a horseshoe kidney catches under the inferior mesenteric artery.

Development of the reproductive system and sex determination
- Gonads start indifferent. In XY embryos, the SRY gene on the Y chromosome triggers a cascade (including SOX9) that makes the gonad a testis.
- Sertoli cells produce anti-Müllerian hormone, which causes the paramesonephric (Müllerian) ducts to regress. Leydig cells make testosterone, which maintains the mesonephric (Wolffian) ducts as epididymis, vas deferens and seminal vesicles. Dihydrotestosterone, formed by 5α-reductase, masculinises the external genitalia and prostate.
- In the absence of these signals, the paramesonephric ducts form the uterine tubes, uterus and upper vagina. Older teaching called female development the "default" pathway, but ovarian development is now known to need active genetic signals (for example WNT4, RSPO1 and FOXL2), so this description is an oversimplification.
- Examples of differences in sex development: androgen insensitivity syndrome (XY, testes present, female external genitalia because androgen receptors do not respond), 5α-reductase deficiency and congenital adrenal hyperplasia.
- The testes descend guided by the gubernaculum, passing through the inguinal canal behind the processus vaginalis; failure gives undescended testis, and a patent processus vaginalis predisposes to indirect hernia or hydrocele.

Exam tips: compare the smooth and striated sphincters (innervation, voluntary control), and be able to explain each step from SRY to male external genitalia.

notes.h: Lower limb: hip, gluteal region, knee, leg, foot and locomotion
notes.body:
The lower limb is built for weight-bearing and walking, so stability matters more than in the upper limb. Exam questions often combine anatomy with a gait abnormality.

Hip and femoral triangle
- The hip joint is a deep ball-and-socket joint; the acetabular labrum and strong ligaments (iliofemoral, pubofemoral, ischiofemoral) make it very stable.
- The head of the femur is supplied mainly by branches of the medial and lateral circumflex femoral arteries that run up the neck; a displaced intracapsular neck fracture can cut these off, risking avascular necrosis of the head.
- The femoral triangle (inguinal ligament, sartorius, adductor longus) contains, from lateral to medial, the femoral nerve, artery and vein and the femoral canal (with lymphatics). Femoral hernias pass through the femoral canal below and lateral to the pubic tubercle and are more common in women.

Gluteal region
- Gluteus maximus (inferior gluteal nerve) extends the hip, for example when climbing stairs or rising from sitting.
- Gluteus medius and minimus (superior gluteal nerve) abduct the hip and, crucially, stabilise the pelvis when standing on one leg. If they are weak, the pelvis drops on the opposite side when standing on the affected leg (positive Trendelenburg sign).
- The sciatic nerve usually leaves the pelvis below piriformis. Intramuscular injections are given in the upper outer quadrant of the buttock to avoid it.

Thigh
- Anterior compartment (quadriceps, sartorius): femoral nerve; quadriceps extends the knee (sartorius flexes hip and knee).
- Medial compartment (adductors): mainly obturator nerve.
- Posterior compartment (hamstrings): sciatic nerve (tibial part, except the short head of biceps femoris from the common fibular part); they flex the knee and (except the short head of biceps femoris, which crosses only the knee) extend the hip.

Knee
- A modified hinge joint between femoral and tibial condyles, with the patella in the quadriceps tendon.
- Anterior cruciate ligament prevents anterior translation of the tibia on the femur (anterior drawer and Lachman tests); posterior cruciate ligament prevents posterior translation.
- Medial and lateral collateral ligaments resist valgus and varus stress. The medial meniscus is attached to the medial collateral ligament and is less mobile, which is often given as a reason why it is injured more often overall. The classic "unhappy triad" (ACL, MCL and medial meniscus) is still taught, but studies suggest the lateral meniscus is more often torn in acute ACL injury.
- Locking: at full extension the femur rotates medially on the tibia to lock the knee; popliteus unlocks it.

Leg and foot
- Anterior compartment (dorsiflexors, toe extensors): deep fibular nerve. Lateral compartment (fibularis longus and brevis, evertors): superficial fibular nerve. Posterior compartment (gastrocnemius, soleus, deep flexors): tibial nerve.
- The common fibular nerve winds round the neck of the fibula, where it is easily injured (fracture, tight plaster), causing foot drop and a high-stepping gait.
- Compartment syndrome: raised pressure in a closed fascial compartment threatens muscle and nerves and is an emergency.
- The foot has medial and lateral longitudinal arches and a transverse arch, maintained by bone shape, ligaments (including the plantar aponeurosis) and muscles.

Veins
- The great saphenous vein runs anterior to the medial malleolus and joins the femoral vein at the saphenous opening; the small saphenous vein runs behind the lateral malleolus to the popliteal vein. Deep veins rely on the calf muscle pump; stasis predisposes to deep vein thrombosis.

Exam tips: for each gait abnormality (Trendelenburg, foot drop, weak quadriceps), name the muscle, nerve and likely site of injury.

cards.b: Ventral rami of C5, C6, C7, C8 and T1.
Upper (C5–C6), middle (C7) and lower (C8–T1).

cards.f: Why are the cords called lateral, posterior and medial?
cards.b: They are named by their position relative to the second part of the axillary artery, behind pectoralis minor.

cards.f: Rotator cuff muscles and main actions
cards.b: Supraspinatus (abduction), infraspinatus and teres minor (lateral rotation), subscapularis (medial rotation). Together they hold the humeral head in the glenoid.
Upper trunk (C5–C6) injury: arm adducted and medially rotated, elbow extended, forearm pronated ('waiter's tip').
Weak serratus anterior from long thoracic nerve (C5–C7) injury; the medial border of the scapula lifts off the chest wall, especially when pushing against a wall.

cards.f: Nerve at risk in surgical neck fracture of the humerus
cards.b: Axillary nerve (with the posterior circumflex humeral artery): weak deltoid and teres minor, numb skin over lower deltoid.
Median nerve plus nine tendons: 4 flexor digitorum superficialis, 4 flexor digitorum profundus and flexor pollicis longus.

cards.f: Cubital fossa contents, lateral to medial
cards.b: Biceps tendon, brachial artery, median nerve (radial nerve under the lateral border).

cards.f: Nerve at risk in mid-shaft humeral fracture
cards.b: Radial nerve in the radial (spiral) groove: wrist drop and sensory loss over the dorsal first web space.

cards.f: Why does scaphoid fracture risk avascular necrosis?
cards.b: Blood vessels enter the scaphoid mainly distally, so a waist fracture can cut off supply to the proximal pole.
Abductor pollicis brevis, flexor pollicis brevis, opponens pollicis: recurrent branch of the median nerve.
A proximal (elbow) ulnar lesion causes less clawing than a wrist lesion because the medial flexor digitorum profundus is also paralysed, so the fingers are not pulled into flexion.

cards.f: Actions of palmar and dorsal interossei
cards.b: Palmar adduct (PAD), dorsal abduct (DAB) the fingers relative to the axis of the middle finger; all supplied by the ulnar nerve.
Endoneurium surrounds each axon, perineurium each fascicle (contributes to the blood–nerve barrier) and epineurium the whole nerve.
Conduction block with intact axon (e.g. from compression); full recovery in days to weeks.
Axon divided but sheaths intact; Wallerian degeneration occurs but regrowth is guided, so recovery is usually good though slow.
Complete division of the nerve including its sheaths; needs surgical repair and recovery is often incomplete.
Breakdown of the axon and myelin distal to an axonal injury, with debris cleared by Schwann cells and macrophages.
Columns of proliferating Schwann cells in the distal stump that guide regenerating axon sprouts.

cards.f: Approximate rate of peripheral axon regrowth
cards.b: Often quoted as about 1 mm per day; actual rates vary with age, site and type of injury.

cards.f: Dermatome landmarks: T4, T10, C6, S1
cards.b: T4 nipple, T10 umbilicus, C6 thumb, S1 lateral border and sole of the foot.
Somites: sclerotome (vertebrae, ribs), myotome (skeletal muscle) and dermatome (dermis of the back).
Kidneys, gonads and their duct systems.
Somatopleure: somatic lateral plate mesoderm + ectoderm, forms the body wall. Splanchnopleure: splanchnic mesoderm + endoderm, forms the gut wall.

cards.f: What does the intraembryonic coelom become?
cards.b: The pericardial, pleural and peritoneal cavities.
Each vertebra forms from the caudal half of one sclerotome and cranial half of the next, so spinal nerves exit between vertebrae.
Part of the nucleus pulposus of the intervertebral discs.
Epaxial: deep back muscles, dorsal rami. Hypaxial: body wall and limb muscles, ventral rami.
Primary (thoracic and sacral kyphoses) present in the fetus; secondary (cervical and lumbar lordoses) develop with head control and walking.
Flat bones of the skull vault and much of the clavicle; bone forms directly in mesenchyme without a cartilage model.

cards.f: Which root does a posterolateral L4/L5 disc herniation usually compress?
cards.b: The L5 root, which descends past the disc to exit at the L5/S1 foramen.
Outer annulus fibrosus (concentric fibrocartilage lamellae) surrounding a gelatinous nucleus pulposus.
Elastic ligament joining laminae of adjacent vertebrae; helps restore the flexed spine to the upright position.
Foramina transversaria in the transverse processes, transmitting the vertebral arteries (usually from C6 upwards).
Stance (heel strike to toe off, about 60% of the cycle in walking) and swing (about 40%).

cards.f: Order of the intercostal neurovascular bundle
cards.b: Vein, artery, nerve from superior to inferior, in the costal groove under each rib.

cards.f: Why does an aspirated foreign body usually enter the right lung?
cards.b: The right main bronchus is wider, shorter and more vertical than the left.
Second costal cartilage; boundary of superior and inferior mediastinum (about T4/T5); tracheal bifurcation and arch of aorta are near this level.

cards.f: Why is the diaphragm supplied by C3–C5?
cards.b: Its main precursor, the septum transversum, forms opposite the cervical segments and carries its phrenic nerve supply as it descends.
Septum transversum, pleuroperitoneal membranes, dorsal mesentery of the oesophagus and muscle from the body wall.
Pulmonary resistance falls and left atrial pressure rises above right, pressing septum primum against septum secundum.
Defined by which artery gives the posterior interventricular artery; most often the right coronary, but this varies.

cards.f: Most common side of congenital diaphragmatic hernia
cards.b: Left posterolateral, through a defect in the pleuroperitoneal membrane.

cards.f: Layers of the anterior abdominal wall (lateral part)
cards.b: Skin, superficial fascia, external oblique, internal oblique, transversus abdominis, transversalis fascia, extraperitoneal fat, parietal peritoneum.
Indirect: through the deep ring lateral to the inferior epigastric vessels. Direct: through the posterior wall medial to them (Hesselbach's triangle).

cards.f: Arteries of foregut, midgut and hindgut
cards.b: Coeliac trunk, superior mesenteric artery and inferior mesenteric artery respectively.

cards.f: Referred pain from foregut, midgut, hindgut
cards.b: Epigastric, periumbilical and suprapubic regions respectively.
About 270° anticlockwise (viewed from the front) around the superior mesenteric artery, during physiological herniation and return (about weeks 6–12).
The opening connecting the greater sac with the lesser sac, lying behind the free edge of the lesser omentum.
Organs that had a mesentery and lost it: most of the duodenum, pancreas, ascending and descending colon.
Thoracolumbar: lateral horn of spinal segments T1–L2.
Craniosacral: cranial nerves III, VII, IX, X and sacral segments S2–S4.
White: myelinated preganglionic fibres into the chain, only at T1–L2. Grey: unmyelinated postganglionic fibres back to every spinal nerve.

cards.f: Why is the adrenal medulla unusual?
cards.b: It receives preganglionic sympathetic fibres directly; its chromaffin cells act as modified postganglionic neurons releasing mainly adrenaline into the blood.

cards.f: Exception to noradrenergic sympathetic postganglionic fibres
cards.b: Sympathetic fibres to most sweat glands release acetylcholine (muscarinic receptors).
Interrupted sympathetic supply to the head: ptosis, miosis and loss of sweating on the same side of the face.
Lymph from the lower body and left side of the upper body into the junction of the left internal jugular and left subclavian veins.
Air, fat, soft tissue/fluid, bone, metal.
Loss of a normal border on a radiograph because a structure of similar (soft-tissue) density lies against it, e.g. right middle lobe consolidation obscuring the right heart border.

cards.f: Why not judge heart size on an AP chest film?
cards.b: In AP projection the heart is further from the detector and is magnified.

cards.f: Hounsfield units of water and air
cards.b: Water 0 HU; air about −1000 HU; bone strongly positive.
T1: fat bright, fluid dark. T2: fluid bright. Use the fluid signal to tell them apart.
Viewed from the patient's feet: patient's right on the viewer's left.
Anechoic (black), often with posterior acoustic enhancement.
Puborectalis, pubococcygeus and iliococcygeus.

cards.f: Nerve supply of the external anal and urethral sphincters
cards.b: Pudendal nerve (S2–S4); striated muscle under voluntary control.
Pelvic splanchnic nerves from S2–S4; causes bladder contraction during voiding.
It slings round the anorectal junction to keep the anorectal angle; relaxation straightens the angle for defecation.
Ureter, renal pelvis, calyces and collecting ducts; the metanephric mesenchyme forms the nephrons.
Secreted by fetal Sertoli cells; causes regression of the paramesonephric (Müllerian) ducts.
XY individual with testes and testosterone, but non-functional androgen receptors; female external genitalia and no uterus (AMH still acts).
Older teaching said so, but ovarian development needs active signals (e.g. WNT4, RSPO1, FOXL2), so 'default' is now seen as an oversimplification.

cards.f: Contents of femoral triangle, lateral to medial
cards.b: Femoral nerve, femoral artery, femoral vein, femoral canal (lymphatics).
When standing on the affected leg the pelvis drops on the opposite side: weak gluteus medius/minimus or superior gluteal nerve lesion on the stance side.

cards.f: Main blood supply to the femoral head in adults
cards.b: Retinacular branches of the medial and lateral circumflex femoral arteries (mainly medial) running along the neck.

cards.f: Nerve injured in fibular neck fracture
cards.b: Common fibular nerve: foot drop (loss of dorsiflexion and eversion) and sensory loss over the dorsum of the foot.

cards.f: Function of the anterior cruciate ligament
cards.b: Prevents anterior translation of the tibia on the femur; tested by the anterior drawer and Lachman tests.

cards.f: Safe site for gluteal intramuscular injection
cards.b: Upper outer quadrant of the buttock, away from the sciatic nerve.
Anterior: deep fibular. Lateral: superficial fibular. Posterior: tibial.
Popliteus, by laterally rotating the femur on the tibia (or medially rotating the tibia) at the start of flexion.

questions.q: A newborn delivered after shoulder dystocia holds the arm adducted and medially rotated with the forearm pronated. Which part of the brachial plexus is most likely injured?
questions.why: Traction that widens the angle between neck and shoulder tears the upper trunk, losing abductors and lateral rotators of the shoulder and elbow flexors and supinators, giving the 'waiter's tip'. A lower trunk lesion mainly affects the small muscles of the hand. A posterior cord lesion would cause weakness of extensors (radial and axillary nerves) without this posture, and a medial cord lesion affects ulnar-supplied muscles and the median nerve's medial-cord fibres to the hand, again without this posture.

questions.q: Which muscle is supplied by the nerve that is most at risk in an anterior dislocation of the shoulder?
questions.why: The axillary nerve runs round the surgical neck close to the inferior capsule and is stretched in anterior dislocation; it supplies deltoid and teres minor. Biceps is supplied by the musculocutaneous nerve, serratus anterior by the long thoracic nerve and latissimus dorsi by the thoracodorsal nerve.

questions.q: Outline the organisation of the brachial plexus from roots to terminal branches, naming the five main terminal branches and the cord each comes from.
markScheme: Roots: ventral rami C5–T1
Trunks: upper C5–6, middle C7, lower C8–T1; each splits into anterior and posterior divisions
Cords named relative to the axillary artery: lateral, posterior, medial
Branches: musculocutaneous (lateral), median (lateral and medial), ulnar (medial), axillary and radial (posterior)
Anterior divisions supply flexor compartments, posterior divisions extensors
questions.modelAnswer: The plexus is formed by the ventral rami of C5 to T1. These join to form three trunks: upper (C5–C6), middle (C7) and lower (C8–T1). Each trunk divides into an anterior division, which will supply flexor compartments, and a posterior division, which will supply extensor compartments. The divisions regroup into three cords named by their relation to the axillary artery: the lateral cord (anterior divisions of upper and middle trunks), the medial cord (anterior division of the lower trunk) and the posterior cord (all three posterior divisions). The lateral cord gives the musculocutaneous nerve, the medial cord the ulnar nerve, the lateral and medial cords together form the median nerve, and the posterior cord ends as the axillary and radial nerves.

questions.q: A patient has numbness of the palmar thumb, index and middle fingers with thenar wasting, but normal sensation over the thenar eminence itself. Where is the nerve most likely compressed?
options: In the radial groove of the humerus
questions.why: The palmar cutaneous branch of the median nerve leaves before the carpal tunnel and passes superficial to the flexor retinaculum, so carpal tunnel compression spares skin over the thenar eminence. A median lesion in the cubital fossa would also numb the thenar skin and weaken long forearm flexors. The ulnar nerve runs behind the medial epicondyle and the radial nerve in the radial groove; neither supplies the palmar skin of the thumb, index and middle fingers or the thenar muscles that waste here (abductor pollicis brevis and opponens pollicis are median-supplied).

questions.q: Which muscle is NOT supplied by the ulnar nerve?
questions.why: Opponens pollicis is a thenar muscle supplied by the recurrent branch of the median nerve. Adductor pollicis, all the interossei and flexor carpi ulnaris are supplied by the ulnar nerve.

questions.q: A cyclist falls on an outstretched hand and has pain in the anatomical snuffbox. Explain the likely injury, why follow-up matters even if the first X-ray is normal, and the anatomical basis of the main complication.
markScheme: Likely scaphoid fracture (commonest carpal fracture; snuffbox tenderness)
Fractures may not be visible on initial radiographs; repeat imaging or MRI/CT is used
Blood supply enters mainly distally (retrograde supply)
Waist or proximal fracture can leave the proximal pole avascular
Complications: avascular necrosis, non-union, later wrist arthritis
questions.modelAnswer: A fall on the outstretched hand with snuffbox tenderness suggests a scaphoid fracture, the commonest carpal fracture. These are often invisible on the first radiographs, so the wrist is usually immobilised and re-imaged, or MRI or CT is used, rather than discharging the patient. The key anatomical point is that the scaphoid's blood supply enters mainly at its distal end and runs proximally, so a fracture through the waist can cut off the proximal pole, which may then undergo avascular necrosis or fail to unite, leading to collapse and later osteoarthritis of the wrist.

questions.q: In axonotmesis, which of the following is preserved?
options: The endoneurial tubes and connective tissue sheaths
questions.why: Axonotmesis means the axons are divided but the sheaths remain intact, which is why regrowth is guided and recovery is usually good. The axon itself is broken, the distal myelin undergoes Wallerian degeneration and conduction across the lesion is lost; preserved axonal continuity with conduction block would be neurapraxia.

questions.q: Which cell forms myelin around peripheral nerve axons?
questions.why: Schwann cells myelinate peripheral axons, one internode each. Oligodendrocytes myelinate CNS axons, astrocytes support CNS neurons and form part of the blood–brain barrier, and satellite cells surround neuron cell bodies in ganglia.

questions.q: Describe the events in a peripheral nerve after it is crushed so that the axons are divided but the sheaths are intact, and explain why a lesion high in the arm recovers less well than one at the wrist.
markScheme: This is axonotmesis
Distal segment undergoes Wallerian degeneration; debris cleared by Schwann cells and macrophages
Cell body shows chromatolysis; Schwann cells form bands of Büngner and secrete trophic factors
Axons regrow along intact endoneurial tubes at roughly 1 mm/day
Proximal lesion: longer distance means target muscles stay denervated longer, atrophy and lose end plates, so recovery is poorer
questions.modelAnswer: Crushing that divides axons but leaves the sheaths intact is axonotmesis. Distal to the lesion the axons and their myelin undergo Wallerian degeneration, and the debris is cleared by Schwann cells and macrophages. The neuronal cell body shows chromatolysis as it switches to making proteins for regrowth. Schwann cells in the distal stump proliferate and form bands of Büngner, and sprouts from the proximal stump grow down the intact endoneurial tubes, which guide them back to their original targets, at roughly a millimetre a day. A lesion high in the arm is a long way from the hand muscles, so they stay denervated for many months; denervated muscle atrophies and its motor end plates degenerate, so even when axons arrive, functional recovery is less complete than after a wrist lesion.

questions.q: Persistence of which embryonic structure gives rise to a Meckel's diverticulum?
questions.why: Meckel's diverticulum is a remnant of the vitelline duct joining the midgut to the yolk sac, found on the antimesenteric border of the ileum. A patent urachus links bladder and umbilicus, the allantois is the urachus's precursor, and a patent processus vaginalis predisposes to indirect inguinal hernia.

questions.q: Why do skeletal muscles of the limbs receive their nerve supply from ventral rami?
options: They develop from lateral plate mesoderm
They develop from neural crest cells
They develop from hypaxial myotome cells that migrate into the limb buds
questions.why: Limb muscle precursors migrate from the hypaxial part of the somites into the limb buds, and hypaxial muscle is supplied by ventral rami. Epaxial muscle forms the deep back muscles (dorsal rami). Lateral plate mesoderm forms the limb's bones and connective tissue but not its muscle, and neural crest forms peripheral neurons, glia and pigment cells, not skeletal muscle of the limbs.

questions.q: Describe the subdivisions of the intraembryonic mesoderm and name the main adult derivatives of each.
markScheme: Paraxial mesoderm forms somites
Sclerotome: vertebrae and ribs; myotome: skeletal muscle; dermatome: dermis of the back
Intermediate mesoderm: kidneys, gonads and genital ducts
Lateral plate splits into somatic and splanchnic layers enclosing the coelom
Somatic: body wall, limb bones and connective tissue; splanchnic: smooth muscle and connective tissue of gut, heart and vessels
Coelom: pericardial, pleural and peritoneal cavities
questions.modelAnswer: Mesoderm either side of the notochord is divided into three strips. Paraxial mesoderm segments into somites; each somite gives a sclerotome that forms the vertebrae and ribs, a myotome that forms skeletal muscle of the back, body wall and limbs, and a dermatome that forms the dermis of the back. Intermediate mesoderm forms the kidneys, the gonads and their ducts. Lateral plate mesoderm splits into a somatic layer, which with the overlying ectoderm makes the body wall and the bones and connective tissue of the limbs, and a splanchnic layer, which with the endoderm forms the gut wall and also the heart and blood vessels. The space between the somatic and splanchnic layers, the intraembryonic coelom, becomes the pericardial, pleural and peritoneal cavities.

questions.q: A posterolateral herniation of the L5/S1 intervertebral disc most commonly compresses which nerve root?
questions.why: The L5 root exits above the L5/S1 disc through the L5/S1 foramen, so a posterolateral herniation catches the S1 root descending to exit below. L4 exits higher still, and S2 lies further medially and lower in the canal, so it is less commonly involved.

questions.q: Which joint is a secondary cartilaginous joint (symphysis)?
options: Joint between two vertebral bodies (intervertebral disc)
questions.why: Intervertebral discs (and the pubic symphysis) are fibrocartilaginous, secondary cartilaginous joints. A growth plate is a primary (hyaline) cartilaginous joint, a suture is fibrous and the knee is synovial.

questions.q: Explain the anatomical reasons why lumbar disc herniations most often occur posterolaterally and what clinical features result.
markScheme: Posterior longitudinal ligament is narrow and thinner laterally
Annulus is thinner posteriorly; nucleus pushed back in flexion
Herniation compresses the traversing nerve root (e.g. L4/5 disc → L5)
Features: back pain with radicular leg pain in a dermatome, myotomal weakness, reduced reflex
questions.modelAnswer: The posterior longitudinal ligament is narrow and does not cover the posterolateral parts of the disc, and the annulus fibrosus is thinner posteriorly, so when the spine is loaded in flexion the nucleus pulposus tends to be pushed backwards and sideways. A posterolateral herniation in the lumbar region usually compresses the root traversing the disc on its way to exit at the level below, so an L4/L5 herniation affects L5. The patient has back pain with sciatica radiating in the corresponding dermatome, possible sensory loss, weakness in that myotome and sometimes a reduced reflex (for an S1 root, the ankle jerk).

questions.q: When a chest drain is inserted through an intercostal space, why is it passed just above the upper border of a rib?
options: Because the intercostal muscles are absent there
To avoid the intercostal vein, artery and nerve that run under the lower border of the rib above
Because the pleura is thinnest there
To avoid the internal thoracic artery
questions.why: The main neurovascular bundle lies in the costal groove under each rib, so keeping close to the top of the rib below avoids it. The pleura is not thinner there, the internal thoracic artery runs near the sternal edge rather than in the drain site, and the intercostal muscles are present across the whole space.

questions.q: Which embryonic event is responsible for a tracheo-oesophageal fistula?
options: Failure of the foramen ovale to close
Incomplete separation of the lung bud from the foregut by the tracheo-oesophageal septum
Failure of closure of the pleuroperitoneal membrane
questions.why: The respiratory tree buds from the ventral foregut and must be separated from the oesophagus by the tracheo-oesophageal septum; incomplete separation leaves a fistula. Pleuroperitoneal membrane failure causes diaphragmatic hernia, a patent foramen ovale is a cardiac defect and midgut malrotation affects the intestine.

questions.q: Describe the changes to the fetal circulation that occur at birth.
markScheme: Lungs expand; pulmonary vascular resistance falls and pulmonary blood flow rises
Placental circulation removed; systemic resistance rises
Left atrial pressure exceeds right; septum primum pushed against septum secundum, functionally closing the foramen ovale
Ductus arteriosus constricts (rising oxygen, falling prostaglandins) and later becomes ligamentum arteriosum
Ductus venosus and umbilical vessels close (ligamentum venosum, ligamentum teres, medial umbilical ligaments)
questions.modelAnswer: Before birth, oxygenated blood from the placenta bypasses the liver through the ductus venosus and the lungs through the foramen ovale and ductus arteriosus. At birth the lungs expand, so pulmonary vascular resistance falls and blood flow through the lungs rises, increasing return to the left atrium. Clamping the cord removes the low-resistance placenta, so systemic resistance rises. Left atrial pressure now exceeds right atrial pressure, pushing the septum primum against the septum secundum and functionally closing the foramen ovale. The ductus arteriosus constricts in response to higher oxygen and falling prostaglandin levels and later becomes the ligamentum arteriosum. The umbilical vessels and ductus venosus close, becoming the medial umbilical ligaments, ligamentum teres and ligamentum venosum.

questions.q: During a hernia repair, the surgeon finds the hernial sac emerging lateral to the inferior epigastric vessels. What type of hernia is this?
questions.why: A sac lateral to the inferior epigastric vessels has entered through the deep inguinal ring, which defines an indirect hernia. A direct hernia lies medial to these vessels in Hesselbach's triangle, a femoral hernia passes below the inguinal ligament through the femoral canal, and an umbilical hernia is at the umbilicus.

questions.q: Early appendicitis classically causes pain first felt around the umbilicus. Why?
options: The appendix is a midgut derivative, and its visceral afferents enter the cord at about the T10 level
The appendix is supplied by the inferior mesenteric artery
The appendix lies directly behind the umbilicus
The parietal peritoneum is inflamed from the start
questions.why: Visceral pain from the midgut is referred to the T10 dermatome around the umbilicus. The appendix is supplied by a branch of the superior mesenteric artery, not the inferior mesenteric, it usually lies in the right iliac fossa, and parietal peritoneal involvement comes later and causes the shift of pain to the right iliac fossa.

questions.q: Describe the normal development of the midgut and explain how abnormal rotation can present in a newborn.
markScheme: Midgut supplied by superior mesenteric artery; extends from second part of duodenum to distal transverse colon
Physiological herniation into umbilical cord around week 6 due to rapid growth
Rotates 270° anticlockwise around SMA and returns by about weeks 10–12
Malrotation: bowel abnormally placed on a narrow mesentery; Ladd's bands may obstruct duodenum
Volvulus: twisting causes bilious vomiting and ischaemia, a surgical emergency
questions.modelAnswer: The midgut runs from the second part of the duodenum to roughly two-thirds of the way along the transverse colon and is supplied by the superior mesenteric artery. Because it grows faster than the abdominal cavity, the midgut loop herniates into the umbilical cord at about week 6. While outside and as it returns, it rotates a total of about 270° anticlockwise (viewed from the front) around the axis of the superior mesenteric artery, so that the caecum ends in the right iliac fossa and the duodenojejunal flexure lies to the left. If rotation is incomplete the bowel sits on a narrow mesenteric base, and peritoneal bands can cross and obstruct the duodenum. The narrow mesentery can twist, causing midgut volvulus, which presents with bilious vomiting and threatens the blood supply of the whole midgut, so it needs urgent surgery.

questions.q: Which statement about the sympathetic chain is correct?
options: Its preganglionic neurons lie in the dorsal horn
Grey rami communicantes connect it to every spinal nerve
White rami communicantes are found at every spinal level
All preganglionic fibres synapse in the chain
questions.why: Grey rami carry postganglionic fibres back to every spinal nerve, so sympathetic fibres reach the whole body wall and limbs. White rami exist only at T1–L2 where preganglionic fibres leave the cord. Splanchnic nerves pass through the chain without synapsing, and preganglionic sympathetic cell bodies are in the lateral horn, not the dorsal horn.

questions.q: Lymph from the right upper limb normally drains into which vessel?
questions.why: The right lymphatic duct drains the right side of the head, neck, thorax and right upper limb. The thoracic duct drains the rest of the body, the cisterna chyli is the abdominal start of the thoracic duct, and the portal vein carries blood, not lymph.

questions.q: Trace the pathway of a sympathetic fibre that causes sweating on the skin of the forearm, and name the transmitter at each synapse.
markScheme: Preganglionic cell body in lateral horn of upper thoracic segments
Leaves via ventral root and spinal nerve, enters chain via white ramus
Ascends in chain and synapses in a cervical/upper thoracic ganglion (e.g. stellate/middle cervical)
Postganglionic fibre returns via grey ramus to the ventral rami forming the brachial plexus and travels in a cutaneous nerve
ACh (nicotinic) at the ganglion; ACh (muscarinic) at the sweat gland
questions.modelAnswer: The preganglionic neuron lies in the lateral horn of the upper thoracic spinal cord (there is no sympathetic outflow from the cervical segments). Its axon leaves in the ventral root, enters the spinal nerve and passes through a white ramus communicans into the sympathetic chain. It ascends in the chain and synapses in a lower cervical or upper thoracic ganglion, releasing acetylcholine onto nicotinic receptors. The postganglionic axon returns to the ventral rami of C5–T1 through grey rami communicantes, travels through the brachial plexus and a cutaneous nerve of the forearm and ends on the sweat glands, where, unusually for a sympathetic fibre, it releases acetylcholine acting on muscarinic receptors.

questions.q: Which imaging modality uses no ionising radiation and provides the best soft-tissue contrast for imaging a torn knee meniscus?
questions.why: MRI uses magnetic fields and radiofrequency pulses, not ionising radiation, and shows menisci and ligaments well. CT, plain radiographs and fluoroscopy all use X-rays and show soft tissues within joints poorly by comparison.

questions.q: On a PA chest radiograph, the right heart border cannot be seen but the right hemidiaphragm is clear. Which lobe is most likely abnormal?
questions.why: The right heart border is formed by the right atrium, which lies against the right middle lobe; consolidation there removes the air–soft tissue interface (silhouette sign). Right lower lobe disease typically obscures the right hemidiaphragm, right upper lobe disease affects the upper mediastinal border, and the left lower lobe borders the left hemidiaphragm and descending aorta.

questions.q: Compare CT and ultrasound for imaging the abdomen, giving two advantages and one limitation of each.
markScheme: CT: fast, cross-sectional, whole abdomen, good in trauma
CT limitation: ionising radiation (and contrast risks)
Ultrasound: no radiation, portable, real-time, cheap; Doppler flow
Ultrasound limitation: operator-dependent, blocked by bowel gas and bone, limited in obese patients
questions.modelAnswer: CT gives rapid, reproducible cross-sectional images of the whole abdomen and pelvis, shows bone, air and soft tissue together and, with intravenous contrast, displays vessels and solid organs, which makes it the main test in major trauma. Its main limitation is the relatively high dose of ionising radiation (with some risks from contrast). Ultrasound is cheap, portable, real-time and free of ionising radiation, so it suits pregnancy, children and bedside use, and Doppler can assess blood flow. However, it depends heavily on the operator's skill, and sound is blocked by bowel gas and bone and weakened in patients with a lot of body fat, so deep structures may be poorly seen.

questions.q: An XY individual with complete androgen insensitivity syndrome would be expected to have which of the following?
options: A well-developed epididymis and vas deferens
questions.why: SRY still makes the gonads testes, and their Sertoli cells secrete anti-Müllerian hormone, so the Müllerian ducts regress and there is no uterus. Without androgen action the Wolffian ducts are not maintained, so the epididymis and vas deferens do not develop properly, and the external genitalia are female. Ovaries would need the absence of SRY.

questions.q: Which structure is smooth muscle under involuntary control and provides most of the resting tone of the anal canal?
questions.why: The internal anal sphincter is a thickening of the circular smooth muscle of the gut wall and supplies most resting tone. The external anal sphincter, puborectalis and iliococcygeus are striated muscles supplied by somatic nerves and under voluntary control.

questions.q: Explain how the genotype XY leads to the development of male internal and external genitalia.
markScheme: SRY on Y chromosome triggers testis development (via SOX9) from the indifferent gonad
Sertoli cells secrete AMH: paramesonephric ducts regress
Leydig cells secrete testosterone: mesonephric ducts become epididymis, vas deferens, seminal vesicles
5α-reductase converts testosterone to DHT
DHT masculinises external genitalia and prostate
Testicular descent guided by gubernaculum through inguinal canal
questions.modelAnswer: The gonad begins indifferent. In an XY embryo the SRY gene on the Y chromosome switches on a cascade, including SOX9, that directs the supporting cells to become Sertoli cells and so makes the gonad a testis. Sertoli cells secrete anti-Müllerian hormone, which causes the paramesonephric ducts to regress, so no uterus or uterine tubes form. Leydig cells secrete testosterone, which maintains the mesonephric ducts and causes them to become the epididymis, vas deferens and seminal vesicles. In the external genital tissues and prostate, 5α-reductase converts testosterone into dihydrotestosterone, which drives fusion of the urogenital folds and growth of the genital tubercle into the penis and of the labioscrotal swellings into the scrotum. Finally the testes descend, guided by the gubernaculum, through the inguinal canal into the scrotum.

questions.q: A patient walks with a high-stepping gait and cannot dorsiflex or evert the foot. Sensation is reduced over the dorsum of the foot. Which nerve is most likely damaged?
questions.why: Loss of dorsiflexion (deep fibular) and eversion (superficial fibular) with dorsal foot numbness points to the common fibular nerve, typically at the fibular neck. The tibial nerve supplies plantarflexors and the sole, the femoral nerve supplies knee extensors, and the superior gluteal nerve supplies hip abductors.

questions.q: Which statement about intracapsular fractures of the femoral neck is correct?
options: They never need surgery because the capsule holds the fragments
They mainly threaten the sciatic nerve
They can interrupt vessels running along the neck to the femoral head, risking avascular necrosis
The femoral head's main supply in adults is the artery in the ligament of the head
questions.why: Retinacular branches of the circumflex femoral arteries run along the neck inside the capsule, so a displaced intracapsular fracture can leave the head avascular. The artery of the ligament of the head contributes little in most adults, these fractures often need surgery, and the sciatic nerve is more at risk in posterior hip dislocation.

questions.q: Explain the anatomical basis of the Trendelenburg sign.
markScheme: Gluteus medius and minimus abduct the hip and stabilise the pelvis in single-leg stance
Supplied by the superior gluteal nerve
In stance on one leg, they contract on the stance side to stop the opposite side of the pelvis dropping
Weakness or nerve injury: pelvis drops on the unsupported (contralateral) side when standing on the affected leg
Patients compensate by leaning the trunk over the affected side (Trendelenburg gait)
questions.modelAnswer: Gluteus medius and gluteus minimus, supplied by the superior gluteal nerve, abduct the hip. Their more important role is to stabilise the pelvis during single-leg stance: when you stand on the right leg, the right gluteus medius and minimus contract to hold the pelvis level and stop the unsupported left side dropping. If these muscles are weak or the superior gluteal nerve is injured (for example by a misplaced injection or surgery), the pelvis drops on the opposite side when the patient stands on the affected leg, which is a positive Trendelenburg sign. When walking, patients compensate by leaning the trunk over the affected side.

questions.q: Using the upper limb as your example, discuss how knowledge of the course and distribution of peripheral nerves allows a clinician to localise a nerve injury. Refer to at least three nerves.
markScheme: Principles: compartments share a nerve; anterior divisions to flexors, posterior to extensors
Brachial plexus organisation and trunk lesions (Erb's and Klumpke's palsies)
Axillary nerve at surgical neck: deltoid weakness, regimental badge numbness
Radial nerve in spiral groove: wrist drop, triceps spared; posterior interosseous lesion spares sensation
Median nerve: carpal tunnel vs elbow lesion (thenar skin sparing; benediction sign)
Ulnar nerve: elbow vs wrist lesion and ulnar paradox
Use of sensory testing, dermatomes vs peripheral nerve territories, and level of branching to localise
Recovery depends on lesion type (Seddon) and distance
questions.modelAnswer:
Peripheral nerves follow predictable courses and give off branches at known levels, so a pattern of weakness and sensory loss can be read like a map. Two principles underlie this. First, muscles in a compartment share a nerve, and in the brachial plexus anterior divisions supply flexor compartments while posterior divisions supply extensors. Second, a lesion affects only structures supplied by branches leaving distal to it, so the most proximal muscle that is spared marks the upper limit of the injury.

At plexus level, traction injuries give root or trunk patterns rather than single-nerve patterns. An upper trunk lesion (Erb's palsy) affects C5–C6 muscles, giving an adducted, medially rotated arm with the forearm pronated. A lower trunk lesion (Klumpke's palsy) weakens the intrinsic hand muscles and may cause Horner's syndrome if T1 sympathetic fibres are damaged. Sensory loss in these cases follows dermatomes rather than peripheral nerve territories.

The axillary nerve winds round the surgical neck of the humerus and is injured in fractures there or in anterior dislocation. Deltoid and teres minor are weak, and a small patch of skin over the lower deltoid is numb.

The radial nerve runs in the spiral groove. A mid-shaft fracture causes wrist drop and loss of finger extension, but triceps is usually spared because its branches arise higher. Sensory loss is over the dorsal first web space. A lesion of the posterior interosseous nerve in the forearm produces finger drop without sensory loss, because the superficial (sensory) branch has already separated.

The median nerve can be compressed in the carpal tunnel, causing thenar weakness and palmar sensory loss in the lateral three and a half digits, but sparing the skin of the thenar eminence, which is supplied by the palmar cutaneous branch arising proximal to the tunnel. A lesion at the elbow also weakens the long flexors of the index and middle fingers and thumb, producing the 'hand of benediction' on attempted fist-making.
