The ulnar nerve is vulnerable behind the medial epicondyle and at the wrist. A wrist lesion paralyses most intrinsic muscles and the medial lumbricals, causing marked clawing of the ring and little fingers. A lesion at the elbow also paralyses the medial half of flexor digitorum profundus, so clawing is paradoxically less marked. Whether sensation on the dorsal medial hand is affected also helps, because the dorsal cutaneous branch arises in the forearm.

Combining these clues (which muscles are spared, whether particular cutaneous branches are involved, dermatomal versus peripheral sensory loss) lets the clinician localise the lesion before nerve conduction studies or imaging. The level also predicts prognosis: in axonotmesis or after repair, axons regrow at roughly a millimetre a day, so proximal lesions take longer and recover less completely because denervated muscle deteriorates in the meantime.

questions.q: "Adult anatomy can only be understood in the light of development." Discuss with reference to the gut, the diaphragm and the inguinal region.
markScheme: Gut tube formed by folding; foregut/midgut/hindgut defined by coeliac, SMA, IMA
Referred visceral pain follows embryological origin (epigastric, periumbilical, suprapubic)
Stomach rotation creates lesser sac and vagal positions; midgut herniation and 270° rotation explain adult position and malrotation/volvulus
Secondary retroperitonealisation explains duodenum and colon positions
Diaphragm components and descent of septum transversum explain C3–5 phrenic supply and referred shoulder tip pain; CDH from pleuroperitoneal failure
Testicular descent and processus vaginalis explain inguinal canal, layers of spermatic cord and indirect hernia
Balanced evaluation: development explains patterns but not all variation; function and mechanics also matter
Clear structure and accurate detail
questions.modelAnswer:
The quotation overstates the case, but development does explain many features of adult anatomy that otherwise look arbitrary, and it predicts many congenital and clinical problems.

The gut. Folding of the embryo in the fourth week incorporates the yolk sac into a gut tube enclosed by splanchnopleure and suspended in the coelom by mesenteries. The tube is divided by its arterial supply: the foregut by the coeliac trunk, the midgut by the superior mesenteric artery and the hindgut by the inferior mesenteric artery. This scheme explains the adult territories of these arteries and also the pattern of referred visceral pain, because afferents from each part enter the cord at the segments of its sympathetic supply: foregut pain is felt in the epigastrium, midgut pain around the umbilicus and hindgut pain suprapubically. Early appendicitis therefore causes periumbilical pain. Rotation of the stomach about its long axis places the left vagus anteriorly and forms the lesser sac behind the stomach. The midgut herniates into the umbilical cord, rotates about 270° anticlockwise around the superior mesenteric artery and returns, which accounts for the caecum lying in the right iliac fossa and for the transverse colon crossing in front of the duodenum. When this fails, malrotation and volvulus result. Fusion of some mesenteries with the posterior wall explains why the duodenum and ascending and descending colon are secondarily retroperitoneal.

The diaphragm. The diaphragm forms from the septum transversum, the pleuroperitoneal membranes, the dorsal mesentery of the oesophagus and body-wall muscle. Because the septum transversum originates opposite the cervical somites, the diaphragm is supplied by the phrenic nerve (C3–C5) even though it ends up at the bottom of the thorax. This explains why irritation of the diaphragm, for example by blood under it, is felt as shoulder-tip pain in the C4 dermatome. Failure of a pleuroperitoneal membrane to close, usually on the left, produces a congenital diaphragmatic hernia, with abdominal contents in the chest and underdeveloped lungs.

The inguinal region. The testis develops in the posterior abdominal wall and descends, guided by the gubernaculum, through the abdominal wall, preceded by a peritoneal pouch, the processus vaginalis. As it passes, it picks up coverings from each layer, giving the internal spermatic fascia (transversalis fascia), cremasteric fascia (internal oblique) and external spermatic fascia (external oblique). The oblique inguinal canal is the track it leaves behind. If the processus vaginalis stays open, abdominal contents can follow the same path as an indirect inguinal hernia, emerging lateral to the inferior epigastric vessels; fluid may collect to form a hydrocele.

Evaluation. These examples show development explaining adult arrangement, nerve supply, referred pain and congenital defects. But development is not the only explanation. Many adult features reflect mechanical function: the arches of the foot, the trabecular pattern of the femoral neck and the shape of joints are shaped by loading. So development is essential for understanding anatomy, but it works best alongside function and clinical reasoning rather than as the only key.
